title: 2025 in LLMs so far, illustrated by Pelicans on Bicycles — Simon Willison
talk_summary: Simon Willison reviews six months of LLM releases using a homemade 'pelican on a bicycle' SVG benchmark, arguing it beats leaderboards for judging model quality. He also covers price collapse across models, tool+reasoning as the key technique, and the 'lethal trifecta' security risk.

takeaways.technique: Cheap custom task-specific eval instead of trusting leaderboards
takeaways.what_they_do: Uses a single hard, self-designed prompt (generate SVG of pelican on bicycle) across every new model, then ranks outputs pairwise with a cheap LLM judge and ELO scoring.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I've been leaning increasingly into my own little benchmark, which started as a joke and has actually turned into something that I I rely on quite a lot.
takeaways.numbers: 500 pairwise matchups judged for 18 cents with GPT-4.1 Mini

takeaways.technique: Pairwise LLM-judge ELO ranking of models
takeaways.what_they_do: Generates side-by-side comparison images, asks a cheap model to pick the better one with a rationale in JSON, then computes ELO chess rankings from 500 matchups.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I ran this last night against 500 comparisons and I did the classic ELO chess ranking scores and now I've got a leaderboard.

takeaways.technique: Track price-per-capability, prefer cheap capable tiers
takeaways.what_they_do: Notes prices of good models crashed ~500x in 3 years and that mid-tier cheap models (GPT-4.1 Mini/Nano, Gemini 2.5 Pro) now match expensive flagships on real tasks; expensive flagships like GPT-4.5 were 750x price for marginal gain.
takeaways.evidence_quote: GPT 4.1 Mini is my default for API stuff now. It's dirt cheap. It's very capable.
takeaways.numbers: GPT-4.5 $75/M input vs GPT-4 Nano 750x cheaper; good-model prices down ~500x in 3 years

takeaways.what_they_do: Reasoning models run a tool, judge whether results are good, tweak the call, and iterate until a result is reached — the combination of tools and reasoning is the highest-leverage pattern.
takeaways.evidence_quote: They can run a search, reason about if it gave them good results, tweak the search, try it again, keep on going until they get to a result.

takeaways.what_they_do: Flags the dangerous combination of private data access + exposure to untrusted instructions + an exfiltration channel; also shows system-prompt tweaks ('be direct, avoid sycophantic flattery') as the fix for bad behavior.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the lethal trifecta, which is when you have an AI system that has access to private data and you expose it to malicious instructions... and there's a mechanism to exfiltrate stuff.

takeaways.technique: System-prompt diffing and explicit anti-sycophancy instructions
takeaways.what_they_do: When a model over-flattered, the fix was a system-prompt edit ('be direct, avoid ungrounded or sycophantic flattery'); leaked prompts let people diff and learn from changes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The cure to sick of fancy is you tell the bot don't be sick of fantic. That's prompt engineering.
